blocks.text: A mechanism is the pathway adapted by a reaction showing the breaking and making of bonds in the substrate leading to the formation of the product. Depending upon the nature of reagents, reaction mechanisms are divided into two main types.
It involves homolysis during which free radicals are produced which attach the substrate molecule e.g.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The free radicals attack the substrate molecule.

This reaction proceeds through the free radical mechanim, which was already discussed in Chemistry 11. The reaction involves initiation where initial free radicals are produced. These radicals generate more radicals in the propagation step. Finally, the reaction terminates by combining the free radicals of the same or different types.
It involves heterolysis, during which electrophiles and nucleophiles are produced, which may attack polar substrate molecules. The polar mechanism is further divided into the following types.
In this type of reaction, a nucleophile attacks on a saturated electrophilic carbon and substitutes another nucleophile called leaving group e.g.

blocks.alt: H-O- (nucleophile, with a lone pair) attacks the carbon of bromomethane (H on a dashed bond, H on a wedge, H on a plain bond; C +delta, Br -delta); a curved arrow goes from O to C and another from the C-Br bond to Br. This gives a bracketed transition state with charge (-): HO, C and Br joined by dashed lines, three H on C, HO and Br -delta, C +delta. It then gives methanol, H-O-C with three H, plus Br- (leaving group).
blocks.caption: Nucleophilic substitution: hydroxide ion and bromomethane give methanol through a transition state (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In this type of reactions, a nucleophile attacks on electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl compound to give addition product e.g.

blocks.alt: N triple-bond C- with a lone pair attacks the +delta carbon of ethanal (C=O with O -delta, H3C and H on the carbon); one curved arrow goes from the lone pair to C and another from the C=O bond to O. This gives N-C-C(H)(CH3) with O- carrying lone pairs. With H-CN (+delta H, -delta CN) it gives 2-hydroxy propanenitrile, N-C-C(OH)(CH3)-H, plus CN-.
blocks.caption: Nucleophilic addition: cyanide ion adds to ethanal, giving 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In this type of reaction, an electrophile attacks on an electron rich position (nucleophilic) like carbon-carbon double or triple bond e.g.

blocks.alt: H2C=CH2 (ethene) plus H-Br with H +delta and Br -delta; a curved arrow runs from the C=C double bond to H. The arrow leads to CH3-CH2-Br (bromoethane).
blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition: ethene and hydrogen bromide give bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In this type of reaction, two atoms or groups are removed from two adjacent carbon atoms in molecule. The removal results in the formation of a double or triple bond.

blocks.alt: HO- with a lone pair plus bromoethane, drawn as CH2-CH2-Br with an H above the first carbon; the carbon bonded to Br is +delta and Br -delta. Three curved arrows: from the HO- lone pair to the H, from the C-H bond to the C-C bond, and from the C-Br bond to Br. The products are CH2=CH2 (ethene) + H2O + Br-.
blocks.caption: Elimination: hydroxide ion and bromoethane give ethene, water and bromide ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed scheme marks the CH2 bonded to Br as -delta; bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so that carbon is +delta, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Quick Check 19.6
blocks.text:
a) Describe each of the following as electrophile, nucleophile or free radical.
i) NH₃
ii) Br
iii) H₂O
iv) NO₂⊕
v) Clδ⊕
b) Classify each of these reactions as addition, substitution, elimination or rearrangement.
(i) CH₃CH = CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃
(ii) CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr
(iii) CH₃CH₂CHClCH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH = CH₂ + HCl
c) Classify the following reactions into one (or more) of the following six categories:
Substitution, addition, hydrolysis, reduction, condensation, oxidation.
(i) (CH₃)₂C=O + H₂N–NH₂ → (CH₃)₂C = N – NH₂ + H₂O
(ii) CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH
